meta.title: Who really said "My actions are my only true belongings. I cannot escape the consequences of my actions"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A real Buddhist teaching in modern English. The doctrine is canonical; the sentence is Thich Nhat Hanh’s, from No Death, No Fear (2002).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My actions are my only true belongings. I cannot escape the consequences of my actions'?
meta.ogDescription: The fifth of the Five Remembrances — but not in these words. The canonical line reads “I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions.”

answer.label: Thích Nhất Hạnh’s wording of a canonical teaching
answer.authorDates: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, poet and peace activist
answer.sourceLine: Both halves of this are true and they pull in different directions. The teaching is canonical: it is the fifth of the Five Remembrances, from the Upajjhatthana Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 ↗), which Thanissaro Bhikkhu translates as “I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my arbitrator.” The sentence is modern. It comes from Thích Nhất Hạnh’s No Death, No Fear (Riverhead, 2002), pp. 149–150, where the remembrances are laid out as a guided breathing practice: “Breathing in, I know that my actions of body, speech and mind are my only true belongings. Breathing out, I know I cannot escape the consequences of my actions.” Strip the breathing and you have the quote in circulation.
answer.confidenceText: Right doctrine, modern words, wrong speaker

docMeta.dd: No Death, No Fear: Comforting Wisdom for Life
Thích Nhất Hạnh · New York: Riverhead Books · 2002 · pages 149–150
Upajjhatthana Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 — the Five Remembrances
“I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my arbitrator.” (Thanissaro)

source.excerpt: Breathing in, I know that my actions of body, speech and mind are my only true belongings. Breathing out, I know I cannot escape the consequences of my actions.
trail: Downloaded and searched the full text of No Death, No Fear on the Internet Archive ↗. The phrase “true belongings” occurs in the guided contemplation of the Five Remembrances at pages 149–150, in the two-line breathing form quoted above.

Established the canonical source and its standard translation from Wikipedia’s article on the Upajjhatthana Sutta ↗, which sets out the five remembrances of Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 and gives Thanissaro’s and Nyanaponika & Bodhi’s renderings of the fifth side by side.

Checked Nhất Hạnh’s own liturgical rendering for comparison. In Chanting from the Heart ↗ (Plum Village, 2006) the fifth remembrance reads “I inherit the results of my actions of body, speech, and mind. My actions are my continuation” — a third wording again, from the same teacher.

Confirmed the phrase is associated with him independently: Wikiquote’s Thích Nhất Hạnh page ↗ quotes Cherríe Moraga’s A Xicana Codex of Changing Consciousness (2011) writing “Our actions are our only true belongings, counsels Thich Nhat Hanh.”
source.excerptNote: The popular quote is this passage with the scaffolding removed. “Breathing in, I know that…” becomes a flat declarative; “my actions of body, speech and mind” shortens to “my actions.” Nothing false is introduced — but what began as an instruction to a practitioner ends up looking like a pronouncement transcribed from scripture.

author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Thiền Buddhist monk, poet and peace activist
author.bio: Thích Nhất Hạnh — born Nguyễn Xuân Bảo in Huế, Vietnam, in 1926 — was a Thiền Buddhist monk, poet and peace activist who became one of the most widely read Buddhist writers in the English language. Exiled from South Vietnam in 1966 for refusing to take a side in the war, he was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King, Jr. the following year, founded the Plum Village monastery in southwest France in 1982, and is credited with coining the term “engaged Buddhism.” His gift was rendering Buddhist teaching in plain, warm English — which is precisely why so many sentences that are his now circulate under the Buddha’s name.

misattribution.heading: Right doctrine, wrong speaker
misattribution.intro: This one deserves more care than a straight debunk. Unlike most quotations pinned on the Buddha, the teaching here really is his — it is a numbered discourse in the Pali Canon. What is modern is the English.

items.why: The fifth of the Five Remembrances, which Wikipedia sets out with two standard translations ↗: “I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my arbitrator.”
No Death, No Fear ↗, pp. 149–150, as a breathing contemplation: “Breathing in, I know that my actions of body, speech and mind are my only true belongings…”

items.scope: Even he did not fix the wording
items.why: Nhất Hạnh’s own Plum Village liturgy ↗ gives the fifth remembrance as “I inherit the results of my actions of body, speech, and mind. My actions are my continuation” — which shows there is no single fixed English sentence to attribute to anyone.

misattribution.truthLine: So do not call it a fake, and do not call it the Buddha’s English. Credit Thích Nhất Hạnh ↗ for the sentence and AN 5.57 ↗ for the teaching, and both claims are true.

context.heading: What gets lost when the breathing is removed
lead: The Five Remembrances are not aphorisms. They are a practice: five facts — I will grow old, I will fall ill, I will die, I will be parted from everything I love, and my actions are what remain — to be recited deliberately and often, precisely because the mind avoids them. The Pali discourse says they should be reflected on “whether one is a woman or a man, lay or ordained.”

Thích Nhất Hạnh’s contribution was to pair each with a breath, which is what turns a list of facts into something a person can actually sit with. Cut the breathing out and the fifth remembrance becomes a nice line about personal responsibility. That is not wrong, exactly — it is just much smaller than what it was for.
context.detailsSummary: Why three versions of one sentence exist
detailsBody: There is no authoritative English text of the Five Remembrances, and Nhất Hạnh himself used at least two renderings: the breathing form in No Death, No Fear (2002) and the liturgical form in Chanting from the Heart (2006), where the fifth reads “My actions are my continuation.” Standard scholarly translations differ again.

That variability is normal for translated scripture and is worth remembering whenever a Buddhist quotation appears online in a single, fixed, perfectly polished sentence. A fixed English sentence is usually a sign of a modern author, not an ancient one.
context.pull: A fixed, perfectly polished English sentence is usually a sign of a modern author, not an ancient one.

sourcesVerified.claim: No Death, No Fear (Riverhead, 2002), pp. 149-150, renders the fifth of the Five Remembrances as a breathing contemplation: "Breathing in, I know that my actions of body, speech and mind are my only true belongings. Breathing out, I know I cannot escape the consequences of my actions."

Wikipedia's Upajjhatthana Sutta article identifies the Five Remembrances as Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 and gives Thanissaro's translation of the fifth as "I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, and have my actions as my arbitrator. Whatever I do, for good or for evil, to that will I fall heir."
Chanting from the Heart (Plum Village, 2006) gives the fifth remembrance as "I inherit the results of my actions of body, speech, and mind. My actions are my continuation."
Wikiquote's Thich Nhat Hanh page quotes Cherrie Moraga, A Xicana Codex of Changing Consciousness (2011): "Our actions are our only true belongings, counsels Thich Nhat Hanh."
Wikiquote's Gautama Buddha page does not contain the phrase 'true belongings' or 'escape the consequences' in any section.
